title: Depreciable Property - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Learn how Depreciable Property is defined and treated under Canadian tax law in our SR&ED investment tax credit glossary.
summary: For Canadian SR&ED claimants, depreciable property such as laboratory equipment and computers is eligible again under Bill C-15 when acquired after December 15, 2024 and used all or substantially all (90% or more) for SR&ED in Canada. Land and buildings remain excluded, and only new property earns the 15% or 35% federal investment tax credit.

body.text: For Canadian SR&ED claimants, depreciable property such as laboratory equipment and computers is eligible again under Bill C-15 when acquired after December 15, 2024 and used all or substantially all (90% or more) for SR&ED in Canada. Land and buildings remain excluded, and only new property earns the 15% or 35% federal investment tax credit.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Canada enacted the most comprehensive expansion of its research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework in more than a decade. On March 26, 2026, federal Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent—following substantive enactment on February 26, 2026—codifying sweeping enhancements to the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Enacted reforms double the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (superseding the $4,500,000 interim proposal from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), widen the prior-year taxable capital phase-out band from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, introduce an elective 3-year average gross revenue phase-out alternative for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), extend the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restore SR&ED eligibility for depreciable capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and qualifying equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024.

Concurrently with federal legislative modernization, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026 providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks, while Federal Budget 2026 (updated November 5, 2026) proposed eliminating certified board-resolution filing requirements for corporate SR&ED elections and agreements. At the provincial level, Québec enacted Bill 6 on December 12, 2025 to replace its legacy R&D credits with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (offering 30% and 20% fully refundable rates across R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital property for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025), and British Columbia permanently repealed its August 31, 2027 SR&ED sunset while harmonizing fully with the federal Bill C-15 expansions.
1. Legislative Trajectory and the 2025–2026 Canadian R&D Tax Overhaul

Canada's R&D tax architecture operates as a dual-tier federal and provincial/territorial regime anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Policy design resides with the Department of Finance Canada, whereas technical and financial administration resides with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) across all jurisdictions except Québec (where Revenu Québec administers provincial fiscal law while relying on the CRA for scientific R&D verification) and Alberta (which administers its own corporate tax grant system). Federally, the SR&ED program delivers two distinct statutory incentives under the Income Tax Act: first, a 100% immediate deduction (or indefinite carryforward) of allowable SR&ED expenditures pooled under subsection 37(1); and second, an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) of 15% or 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures under section 127 and section 127.1, realized as a reduction of federal Part I tax payable, a cash refund, or a combination of both.
Enactment Timeline: From FES 2024 to Bill C-15 and Budget 2026

Auditing corporate tax filings and financial statement tax provisions across 2025 and 2026 requires distinguishing precisely between un-enacted fiscal proposals and enacted statutory law. On December 16, 2024, the federal 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) initially proposed raising the enhanced 35% SR&ED expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, widening taxable capital phase-out thresholds, extending enhanced refundability to eligible Canadian public corporations, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility. Because those FES 2024 proposals were not enacted into law prior to late 2025, the CRA could not administer them during 2025.

On November 4, 2025, the federal government tabled Budget 2025, absorbing the FES 2024 architecture while increasing the enhanced 35% expenditure limit further to $6,000,000. Following House of Commons approval of the budget on November 17, 2025, the government introduced Bill C-15 (An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025, also cited as the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) on November 18, 2025.

For accounting and financial audit purposes, as at December 31, 2025, Bill C-15 had not achieved substantive enactment under Canadian GAAP (including IFRS Accounting Standards) or enactment under US GAAP, precluding calendar-year entities from booking the enhanced SR&ED credits in their Q4 2025 financial statements. Amended Bill C-15 subsequently achieved substantive enactment on February 26, 2026, and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, bringing the modernized SR&ED provisions into full legal force retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and property acquired or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024). Between April and October 2026, the CRA released updated claim forms, corporate schedules, and administrative policies implementing Bill C-15.

Subsequently, Federal Budget 2026 (published through November 5, 2026) projected $930,000,000 in cumulative five-year federal corporate income tax relief from its SR&ED program measures across 2026–2027 through 2030–2031 ($25 million in 2026–2027, $200 million in 2027–2028, $245 million in 2028–2029, $225 million in 2029–2030, and $235 million in 2030–2031). Budget 2026 also proposed eliminating statutory requirements for corporations to file certified copies of corporate resolutions or authorizations when submitting elections or agreements to transfer qualified SR&ED expenditures or allocate SR&ED employee wages and salaries, effective for elections and agreements executed on or after Royal Assent of the implementing legislation.

body.text: 2. Federal Statutory and Regulatory Architecture
Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1)

Eligibility for federal SR&ED tax incentives—and for every harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credit across Canada—is governed by the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. To qualify, activities must be conducted in Canada (subject to narrow outside-Canada wage rules not applicable to specified employees) and constitute a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis across one of three core categories:

items: Basic Research (Paragraph 248(1)(a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Applied Research (Paragraph 248(1)(b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new materials, products, devices, or processes, or improving existing ones, including incremental improvements.

body.text: Conversely, routine and commercial activities are excluded from SR&ED ("excluded work"). Specifically, CRA policy and harmonized statutory rules exclude excess production (any production beyond what is required for the SR&ED), routine quality control (techniques and work that sustain the quality of a product or service to satisfy given requirements), routine regulatory certification testing, and aesthetic or form-based product design (note that while Québec's new CRIC separately incentivizes pre-commercialization product design and initial certification testing provincially, those pre-commercialization activities remain outside the federal subsection 248(1) definition of R&D).
Dual Calculation Structure: Section 37 Pool vs. Section 127 Qualified Expenditures

A foundational principle of Canadian R&D tax auditing is that "allowable SR&ED expenditure" (for income deduction purposes under section 37) and "qualified expenditure" (for Investment Tax Credit purposes under section 127) are legally distinct concepts that must never be treated as interchangeable in tax working papers. An expenditure can enter the section 37 deductible pool at 100% while earning reduced or zero ITCs under section 127—such as arm's length SR&ED contracts and third-party payments (100% deductible under section 37, but restricted to 80% for ITCs), non-arm's length SR&ED contracts (deductible under section 37, 0% ITC absent a Form T1146 transfer), unpaid non-remuneration current expenses at the 180-day mark (retained in section 37, excluded from current-year ITCs), and used SR&ED capital equipment (allowable on Form T661 Line 390 under paragraph 37(1)(b), but barred from earning ITCs as a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b)(iii)). Conversely, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) inclusions enter section 127 qualified expenditures to generate ITCs without ever entering the section 37 deductible expenditure pool.

body.text: 3. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Entity Thresholds, Phase-Out Elections, and Carryovers
Entity Eligibility and Refundability Matrix Under Bill C-15

Under subsection 127(9) and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, both the federal SR&ED ITC percentage and its cash refundability depend on the claimant's legal structure throughout the taxation year.
Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)

Qualifying CCPCs earn the enhanced 35% federal ITC (15% basic rate plus 20% enhancement) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the maximum expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, increasing the maximum annual enhanced credit from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Within this $6,000,000 limit, the 35% ITC earned on current SR&ED expenditures is 100% refundable, whereas the 35% ITC earned on restored capital SR&ED expenditures is 40% refundable (generating an immediate 14% cash refund on capital outlay plus a 21% non-refundable ITC carryforward after offsetting Part I tax).

Qualified expenditures incurred by a CCPC above its expenditure limit earn the 15% basic ITC. If the CCPC also satisfies the "qualifying corporation" income and capital criteria—where combined prior-year taxable income across associated corporations does not exceed the corporation's qualifying income limit calculated under $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000] (with A equal to nil where prior-year taxable capital is $10,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and taxable capital over $10,000,000)—the 15% ITC earned above the expenditure limit is 40% refundable across both current and capital expenditures.
Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Prior to Bill C-15, listing shares on a public stock exchange automatically terminated CCPC status, dropping a Canadian innovator's federal SR&ED incentive from a 35% refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable credit. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 created the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) category under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.6). To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must be resident in Canada, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or qualify as an eligible subsidiary within an ECPC consolidated group), and not be controlled by non-residents—including satisfying a hypothetical aggregation test confirming that even if all shares owned by non-residents were instead owned by one single hypothetical person, the corporation would still not be controlled by that person. Qualifying ECPCs earn the exact same 35% enhanced ITC up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit as CCPCs, with 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures within the limit, and 15% on excess expenditures.
Foreign-Controlled Subsidiaries, Other Corporations, Individuals, Trusts, and Partnerships

Corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs—including Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign parent corporations, Canadian branches of non-resident corporations, and public companies failing the ECPC ownership test—earn the 15% basic federal ITC on unlimited qualified Canadian SR&ED expenditures, with 0% refundability. Startup founders must note that executing a venture equity round that transfers control to non-resident investors or a non-ECPC public company eliminates CCPC eligibility for subsequent taxation years.

Unincorporated individuals (sole proprietorships) and certain trusts earn the 15% basic ITC, with individuals entitled to 40% refundability on remaining credits after offsetting income tax payable (trusts may also designate SR&ED ITCs to beneficiaries). For partnerships, the SR&ED ITC is computed at the partnership level at the 15% basic rate under subsection 127(8) and allocated to eligible active general partners (non-specified members) to claim on their own corporate or individual returns.

body.text: Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Thresholds and the CCPC Gross Revenue Election

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 widened the phase-out ("grind") range on the $6,000,000 expenditure limit from the legacy $10,000,000–$50,000,000 band to $15,000,000–$75,000,000. Two alternative phase-out tests now operate:

items: Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada (CCPC Default — Subsections 127(10.2) & 127(10.21)): By default, a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins decreasing once prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (combined across all associated CCPCs) reaches $15,000,000, and is reduced to nil ($0) at $75,000,000 or more. Associated CCPCs must allocate their single group expenditure limit on T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026), with failure to file an agreement governed by subsection 127(10.4).

Three-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue (Mandatory for ECPCs under Subsection 127(10.6); Elective for CCPCs under Subsections 127(10.31) & 127(10.32)): For ECPCs and their consolidated groups, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out strictly based on average annual gross revenue reported in financial statements over the preceding 3 fiscal years (or actual preceding fiscal years if fewer than three), retaining the full $6,000,000 limit at or below $15,000,000 and reaching nil ($0) at $75,000,000. Crucially, Bill C-15 empowers a single CCPC (subsection 127(10.31)) or an associated group of CCPCs (subsection 127(10.32)) to elect in prescribed form to replace the taxable capital test with this 3-year average gross revenue test. For electing associated CCPCs, average annual financial-statement revenues for the preceding 3 fiscal years must be summed across every corporation in the associated group for the tax year in question, whether or not those corporations were associated throughout the entire three-year lookback period.

body.text: Tax Planning Illustration (Subsection 127(10.31) CCPC Revenue Election): Consider a capital-intensive Canadian clean-tech or life-sciences CCPC that has raised $80,000,000 in equity and debt capital to build pilot facilities (pushing prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada to $80,000,000, above the $75,000,000 elimination ceiling), while generating $12,000,000 in average annual gross revenue over its preceding three fiscal years, and incurring $6,000,000 in current qualified SR&ED expenditures in its 2026 calendar taxation year. Under the default taxable capital rule, its expenditure limit is ground down completely to $0, restricting all $6,000,000 of expenditures to the 15% non-refundable rate ($900,000 non-refundable ITC; $0 cash refund). By filing the subsection 127(10.31) gross revenue election, because its $12,000,000 3-year average gross revenue sits below the $15,000,000 phase-out threshold, the corporation preserves its entire $6,000,000 expenditure limit—earning $2,100,000 in 100% cash-refundable federal ITCs (35% × $6,000,000), an immediate $1,200,000 increase in total credit value and $2,100,000 increase in non-dilutive liquidity.
Carryback, Carryforward, and Deemed Part I Deduction Rules

Unused balances in the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carry forward indefinitely to offset income in future taxation years. Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs carry back 3 preceding taxation years and carry forward 20 subsequent taxation years under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), after which unapplied credits expire. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5), removing the refunded credit from carryback or carryforward availability.

When carrying back an ITC under subsection 127(5), the allowable carryback to any of the 3 prior years is capped at the lesser of: (a) the portion of current-year ITC in excess of the amount deductible against current-year Part I tax otherwise payable (even if the taxpayer elects not to claim the current-year offset, the absorbable portion cannot be carried back); and (b) the prior year's Part I tax otherwise payable in excess of ITCs already available in that prior year. For instance, if a corporation had $10,000 of Part I tax and $6,000 of ITCs in Year 1 ($4,000 remaining tax), and has $12,000 of Part I tax and $15,000 of non-refundable ITCs in Year 2, $12,000 of the Year 2 ITC is absorbable in Year 2, capping the permissible carryback to Year 1 at $3,000 (the lesser of the $3,000 unabsorbable Year 2 ITC and the $4,000 unabsorbed Year 1 tax).
4. Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Methodologies, Restored Capital Assets, and Exclusions
Salaries and Wages, Unpaid Remuneration, and Specified Employees

Employee remuneration governed by the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025) typically forms the primary expenditure base of Canadian claims. Under both the Proxy and Traditional methods, salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in prosecuting SR&ED in Canada qualify as allowable current expenditures. By contrast, administrative salaries and related benefits of personnel whose duties are not all or substantially all (90% or more) directed to prosecuting SR&ED are prescribed exclusions under Income Tax Regulations clause 2902(a)(i)(A), except to the extent directly attributable under Traditional Method subsections 2900(2) or 2900(3). Additionally, because a partner cannot legally be an employee of their own partnership for income tax purposes, amounts paid as "salary" to a partner are treated as partnership income distributions and disallowed as SR&ED wages.

Two strict compliance traps govern SR&ED payroll audits. First, under the 180-day unpaid remuneration rule, salaries or wages incurred in a taxation year must be paid by year-end or within 180 days thereafter; any salary, wage, or remuneration remaining unpaid after 180 days is excluded from both section 127 qualified expenditures and the section 37 deductible SR&ED pool. Second, heightened restrictions apply to any specified employee—including any employee who does not deal at arm's length with the claimant. For specified employees, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are completely excluded; total allowable SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE); any salary for SR&ED work performed outside Canada is disallowed; and when computing the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base on Form T661 Part 5 (Line 858), each specified employee's includible salary is further capped by the statutory formula 2.5 × A × B ÷ 365 (representing 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by days employed in the year), which must be shared across associated corporations.
Overhead Election: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

On Form T661 Lines 160 and 162, claimants choose annually between the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) ITA) and the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) ITA). Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not track or claim actual SR&ED overhead or indirect support salaries; instead, it calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Form T661 Part 5 (Line 820) equal to 55% of the eligible directly engaged SR&ED salary base under Income Tax Regulations subsection 2900(4), subject to an overall non-SR&ED corporate expense ceiling under subsection 2900(6). While neither the PPA nor the overhead costs it represents enter the section 37 deductible SR&ED pool (actual rent and overhead are deducted as ordinary business expenses), the 55% PPA enters section 127 qualified expenditures to earn the 15% or 35% federal ITC.

Under the Traditional Method, no PPA is calculated. Instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, allocate, and substantiate actual overhead and other expenditures on Form T661 Line 360 that satisfy Income Tax Regulations subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3): costs must be directly related and incremental to prosecuting SR&ED (meaning they would not have been incurred had SR&ED not occurred, per paragraph 2900(2)(c)), or constitute maintenance, upkeep, and incremental expenses directly attributable to providing SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment (subsection 2900(3)). Allowable Traditional Method items include indirect SR&ED support/supervisory wages, SR&ED travel and training, property taxes and upkeep of dedicated SR&ED facilities/equipment, relocation moving expenses for SR&ED personnel, and taxable benefits tied to recruiting SR&ED staff. Labour-intensive software, engineering, and biotechnology firms generally maximize ITC recovery with minimal audit friction under the Proxy Method, whereas facility-intensive industrial or pilot-plant operators whose incremental utilities and plant upkeep exceed 55% of capped direct payroll may benefit from modelling the Traditional Method.

body.text: Materials, Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

The cost of materials consumed or transformed in prosecuting SR&ED is 100% allowable under both methods. Materials transformed into prototypes, experimental batches, or pilot plants that retain commercial value remain subject to SR&ED ITC Recapture if subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.

Payments under arm's length SR&ED contracts—where a contractor performs SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf, the claimant controls the work, and resulting intellectual property rights belong exclusively to the claimant—are 100% deductible in the section 37 pool and 80% includible in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, provided the performer is a taxable supplier. If a current non-wage expenditure (such as a contractor invoice) remains unpaid 180 days after year-end, it stays in the section 37 pool in Year 1, is deducted on Form T661 Line 520 from Year 1 qualified expenditures, and when subsequently paid, 80% of the identified paid amount is added to qualified expenditures in the year of payment.

Payments under non-arm's length (NAL) SR&ED contracts are deductible in the payer's section 37 pool but earn 0% ITC directly for the payer. To shift ITC eligibility to the payer, both parties must file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026), with the performer reporting the transferred amount on Form T661 Line 540. Auditors must verify two strict statutory rules on Form T1146 transfers: first, the performer cannot transfer more than what its year-end qualified expenditures would be absent the transfer—if it attempts to over-transfer, the Income Tax Act invalidates the transfer so no amount ($0) can be transferred; second, if the payer's taxation year ends earlier than the performer's year-end, the payer's ITC claim is deferred until its first taxation year ending at or after the performer's transfer year-end.

Third-party payments to CRA-approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, granting councils, or tax-exempt resident non-profit SR&ED corporations—where the research institution controls the basic or applied research and the claimant obtains non-exclusive preferential rights to exploit the findings in its business—are 100% deductible under section 37 and 80% eligible for federal ITCs.
Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and Equipment Leases (Post-December 15, 2024)

Reversing the 2014 capital repeal, Bill C-15 restored SR&ED incentives for capital equipment, shared-use equipment, and equipment leases acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), administered under the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026).
1. All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Property (Paragraph 37(1)(b) ITA; Form T661 Line 390)

Expenditures to acquire depreciable property owned by the claimant (such as CNC prototyping machines, 3D printers, environmental chambers, laboratory test instruments, computer workstations, and purchased scientific/engineering software licences) after December 15, 2024 qualify where, at acquisition, the claimant intended either to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value in Canadian SR&ED. Capital cost (Box 782) includes purchase price, installation, customs/excise duties, and freight, and claimants must identify the 10 costliest SR&ED properties per project on Form T661 Line 262. Land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings remain strictly excluded. Under amended subsection 127(11.2) ITA, capital property expenditures are deemed not incurred for ITC purposes until the property becomes available for use (determined without reference to paragraphs 13(27)(c) and 13(28)(d))—prompting specialist tax commentary to note a potential technical position where equipment ordered before December 16, 2024 first became available for use after December 15, 2024, though CRA administrative guidance states flatly that property acquired before December 16, 2024 does not qualify.

Critical Audit Distinction — New vs. Used Capital Equipment: While CRA instructions for Form T661 Line 390 allow both new and used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test into the section 37 deductible SR&ED pool (deemed capital cost allowance, precluding duplicate CCA on Schedule T2SCH8), Income Tax Regulations subparagraph 2902(b)(iii) (current to October 29, 2026) continues to classify "property that has been used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose whatever before it was acquired by the taxpayer" as a prescribed expenditure excluded from subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures. Consequently, used equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 earns 0% federal SR&ED ITC; only brand-new equipment earns the 15% or 35% federal ITC.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) ITA; Form T661 Line 504)

Brand-new depreciable equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test—and is neither Prescribed Depreciable Property (Regulation 2900(11)) nor general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF)—qualifies as First-Term SUE if used primarily (more than 50% of operating time) in Canadian SR&ED from its available-for-use date through the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months thereafter, generating a qualified expenditure of 25% (one-quarter) of capital cost on Line 504 (computed excluding borrowed-money costs and deemed capital cost rules, and after subsection 127(11.6) non-arm's length adjustments). Continuing primary SR&ED use across the second statutory period qualifies an additional 25% of capital cost as Second-Term SUE. SUE capital cost never enters the section 37 pool and is depreciated separately under CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8.
3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Form T661 Lines 350, 355, 360 & Box 759)

Although certain secondary practitioner blogs erroneously claimed Bill C-15 excluded leases, official CRA primary policies (SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, updated June 8, 2026) and enacting Bill C-15 provisions confirm that equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 are restored to SR&ED eligibility. Under the Proxy Method, non-GPOEF leased equipment used ≥90% (ASA) in SR&ED is 100% claimable (Line 350) and equipment used primarily (>50% to <90%) is claimable under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI) (Line 355), whereas casual or hourly machine rentals used ≤50% of operating time are excluded. Under the Traditional Method, ≥90% leased equipment is claimed at 100% on Line 350, and <90% leased equipment is claimable on Line 360 as incremental overhead. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, operating-time usage is measured strictly over the period after December 15, 2024.
Cloud Computing, SaaS Subscriptions, and Bill C-15's Accelerated CCA ("Productivity Super-Deduction")

Practitioner guidance confirms that recurring cloud computing and CAD/SaaS software subscriptions do not qualify as standalone SR&ED expenditures under the Proxy Method (as they are neither direct wages, physical materials, SR&ED contracts, nor physical equipment leases, and are deemed covered by the 55% PPA), whereas under the Traditional Method any non-prescribed "other expenditure" must be proven strictly incremental to SR&ED under Regulation 2900(2)(c). Conversely, computers and software licences bought outright after December 15, 2024 and used ≥90% (ASA) in SR&ED qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures.

For capital assets not claimed under SR&ED (or depreciated via Schedule T2SCH8 alongside SUE), Bill C-15 also enacted what Budget 2025 termed the Productivity Super-Deduction package of accelerated Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) incentives: 100% immediate first-year expensing for qualifying Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software) acquired on or after April 16, 2024 and available for use before January 1, 2027; reinstatement of the Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII) for eligible property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030 (phasing out 2030–2033); and 100% first-year enhanced CCA for eligible manufacturing and processing (M&P) buildings, including eligible additions or alterations, acquired after November 3, 2025 (100% if first used for M&P before 2030, 75% in 2030–2031, 55% in 2032–2033, and 0% after 2033). Taxpayers cannot claim both section 37 SR&ED capital deduction and Schedule 8 CCA on the same ASA asset.
Prescribed Exclusions (Regulation 2902), Assistance Reductions, and 20-Year ITC Recapture

Under Income Tax Regulations section 2902, prescribed expenditures barred from earning SR&ED ITCs include general business administration/management; legal or accounting fees (including patent filing fees and SR&ED claim preparation fees); interest and financing deductions under paragraphs 20(1)(c)–(g); entertainment, advertising, or selling expenses; conference or convention expenses; scientific/technical society membership dues; fines or penalties; payments to acquire rights in or arising out of SR&ED; and charitable deductions under sections 110.1 or 118.1.

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) ITA, all government assistance (including provincial/territorial R&D tax credits and federal grants), non-government assistance, and contract payments received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected by the filing-due date reduce qualified expenditures. Under the Proxy Method, the portion of any provincial/territorial R&D credit attributable to the notional 55% PPA reduces federal qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18), does not reduce the section 37 deductible pool, and must be included directly in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) ITA, if property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned within the preceding 20 taxation years (such as transformed prototype materials, purchased SR&ED components, or post-December 15, 2024 capital/SUE equipment) is sold or converted to commercial use, SR&ED ITC Recapture is added to Part I tax payable on Schedule T2SCH31. Notably, if a prototype or test batch was manufactured in-house, recapture applies strictly to the original cost of purchased raw materials—excluding in-house manufacturing/SR&ED labour and overhead—whereas if a custom component was ordered from an arm's length supplier, the entire supplier price (including vendor labour and profit) is subject to recapture.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Ten Canadian provinces and territories provide corporate R&D tax credits that stack with federal SR&ED, though each provincial credit reduces federal qualified expenditures as government assistance under subsection 127(18). Following federal Bill C-15, provincial responses have split between major modernizers (Québec and British Columbia) and jurisdictions retaining independent caps (Ontario and Alberta).
Québec: New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

Enacted via Québec Bill 6 (substantively enacted November 11, 2025 for Canadian GAAP; enacted December 12, 2025 for US GAAP) and effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC replaces Québec's multiple legacy R&D credits (formerly covering R&D salaries, university/public centre contracts, precompetitive partnerships, and research consortia) with a unified, 100% refundable credit administered by Revenu Québec. Eligible corporations with a Québec establishment earn 30% refundable on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the annual exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and 20% refundable on all qualified expenditures above $1,000,000 without upper limit—regardless of foreign ownership or public listing.

To enter the CRIC calculation, qualified expenditures in a taxation year must exceed an applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount per employee adjusted for the percentage of time each employee spent on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work. Uniquely in Canada, while the CRA continues to perform scientific reviews of harmonized R&D work, the CRIC also covers pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with R&D (Form RD-1029.8.PR-T): regulatory tests, technological validations, and studies for initial commercialization certification/approval; product design (form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and material choice); and quality control system implementation required for initial certification. CRIC qualified expenditures comprise 100% of Québec employee wages, 50% of Québec subcontractor contracts, 50% of payments to eligible Québec public research centres, consortia, or university entities, and 100% of property acquisition (capital equipment) costs (excluding land/buildings and barred from double-dipping with Québec's C3i investment credit or Large Investment Project tax holiday), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T.
British Columbia, Ontario, Alberta, and Other Jurisdictions

In British Columbia, Budget 2026 (tabled February 17, 2026) permanently repealed the B.C. SR&ED credit's August 31, 2027 sunset date and enacted full alignment with federal Bill C-15 retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024: qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs now earn a 10% refundable credit on up to $6,000,000 of B.C. qualified expenditures (phasing out over $15,000,000–$75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and including restored capital expenditures), while other corporations and excess spending earn a 10% non-refundable credit on Form T666 (note that static CRA summary tables temporarily lagged this enacted 2026 B.C. expansion, which is confirmed in CRA's corporate legislative updates and B.C. Budget 2026). Expenditures claimed for B.C. SR&ED are excluded from B.C.'s new 15% M&P ITC.

In Ontario, corporations stack three CRA-administered incentives under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario): the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566) up to a $3,000,000 expenditure limit (phasing out over $500,000–$800,000 of prior-year federal taxable income or $25,000,000–$50,000,000 of specified paid-up capital; specialist commentary as of October 2026 notes Ontario has kept the $3M cap and has not confirmed adding restored capital expenditures to the OITC base); the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario R&D Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule T2SCH508); and the 20% refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedule 568) up to $20,000,000 annually. Alberta administers its refundable Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provincially (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970), paying 8% up to a corporation's prior 2-year average Alberta R&D spending and 20% on incremental spending above that 2-year average on up to $4,000,000 annually (phased out over $10,000,000–$50,000,000 of taxable capital). In Saskatchewan, while older CRA summary text reflects a $1,000,000 CCPC refundable limit at 10% (Schedule T2SCH403), 2026 tax credit reporting notes Saskatchewan doubled its CCPC refundable expenditure ceiling to $2,000,000 effective December 16, 2024 (with a $1,000,000 overall annual credit cap).

body.text: Worked Federal-Provincial Stacking & Subsection 127(18) Reconciliation

To demonstrate the exact statutory interaction of restored capital property, the 55% PPA, subsection 127(18) provincial assistance reductions, and paragraph 12(1)(x) income inclusions, consider a calendar-year 2026 CCPC in British Columbia (prior-year taxable capital below $15,000,000; $0 Part I tax payable) electing the Proxy Method:

items: Incurred 2026 Expenditures: $240,000 in arm's length developer wages directly engaged in SR&ED; $20,000 in consumed prototype materials; $50,000 paid to an arm's length Canadian SR&ED subcontractor (taxable supplier); and $100,000 for brand-new test apparatus acquired and available for use in 2026 and used ≥90% (ASA) in B.C. SR&ED.

Pre-Assistance Qualified Expenditures: $240,000 (wages) + $132,000 (55% PPA on $240,000) + $20,000 (materials) + $40,000 (80% of $50,000 contract) = $432,000 current + $100,000 brand-new ASA capital = $532,000.
B.C. 10% Refundable SR&ED Credit: 10% × $532,000 = $53,200 cash refund ($43,200 on current expenditures, including $13,200 attributable to the $132,000 PPA; plus $10,000 on capital expenditures).

Subsection 127(18) Federal Qualified Expenditure Reduction: Net current qualified expenditures equal $432,000 − $43,200 = $388,800; net capital qualified expenditures equal $100,000 − $10,000 = $90,000; total net federal qualified expenditures equal $478,800.

Federal 35% Enhanced SR&ED ITC: Current expenditures earn 35% × $388,800 = $136,080 (100% refundable = $136,080 cash); capital expenditures earn 35% × $90,000 = $31,500 (40% refundable = $12,600 cash refund + $18,900 non-refundable 20-year ITC carryforward), for $167,580 in federal ITCs.

Combined Recovery & Tax Reconciliation: Combined federal and B.C. credits total $220,780, yielding $201,880 in immediate cash refunds ($53,200 + $136,080 + $12,600) plus $18,900 in carryforwards. Under paragraph 12(1)(x) and paragraph 37(1)(d), the $13,200 B.C. credit earned on the notional PPA is included in taxable income in the year received rather than reducing the section 37 pool, whereas the remaining $40,000 of B.C. credit reduces the $410,000 section 37 deductible pool to $370,000.

body.text: 6. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval, and Direct Innovation Grants
CRA Review Streams, Mandatory Tax Forms, and the 18-Month Statutory Bar

Within the CRA, SR&ED claims are evaluated jointly by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) assessing scientific and technological eligibility (Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors) and Financial Reviewers (FRs) auditing costs, contracts, assistance, and ITC schedules (Financial Claim Review Manual – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers). Following Bill C-15's Royal Assent, the CRA published updated versions of Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, May 15, 2026), T2 Schedule 31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, May 22, 2026), T2 Schedule 49 (May 29, 2026), Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, May 15, 2026), and Form T1146 (May 15, 2026), alongside Form T2038(IND) for individuals.

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 127(9) ITA, a claimant must file both Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing all prescribed information no later than 12 months after its income tax return filing-due date—which equals 18 months after taxation year-end for corporations (for example, a December 31, 2025 corporate year-end must be filed on or before June 30, 2027) and 17.5 months after year-end for individuals. Under subsection 220(2.2) ITA, the Minister of National Revenue has zero statutory discretion to extend this 18-month reporting deadline, and an existing claim cannot be amended to add new projects or unfiled prescribed expenditure lines once the 18-month window expires.
The CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process to give Canadian businesses upfront project certainty prior to committing R&D capital. Submitted digitally through My Business Account before commencing SR&ED work or incurring costs, the application delivers a formal CRA eligibility determination within 8 weeks, supported by one-on-one CRA pre-claim consultations (OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca), dedicated webinars, upgraded SR&ED Client Portal and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool modules, and tailored post-approval verification protocols in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants.
Layering Direct Federal Grants with SR&ED

Businesses frequently pair SR&ED credits with non-dilutive direct federal funding, including the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC-IRAP) (funding SME technology R&D and youth hiring), Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) initiatives such as the Compute Access Fund under Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, CanExport Innovation (reimbursing up to 75% of international R&D partnership development costs up to $75,000), and Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's AgriInnovate Program. Under subsection 127(18) and Form T661 Line 515, direct grants reduce qualified expenditures in Part 4 after the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount has already been computed on the unreduced direct SR&ED salary base in Part 5—allowing Proxy Method claimants to retain the full 35% federal ITC on the 55% PPA even on grant-reimbursed salaries.
7. Judicial Precedents, Audit Substantiation, and Penalty Governance
Federal Court of Appeal Jurisprudence and the Five-Criterion Test

Canadian appellate jurisprudence—anchored by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (and applied across subsequent Tax Court of Canada decisions such as 2023 TCC 35)—coupled with the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (August 13, 2021), requires claimants to prove five cumulative elements to establish subsection 248(1) eligibility:

items: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty: Did a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty exist that could not be resolved through standard practice, publicly available engineering knowledge, or routine debugging?
Hypothesis Formulation: Were specific scientific or technological hypotheses formulated specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?

Systematic Investigation (Experiment or Analysis): Did the procedure adhere to a systematic investigation consistent with the scientific method, testing hypotheses through structured experiment or analysis rather than intuitive trial-and-error (as reinforced in National R&D, 2022 FCA 72)?

Scientific or Technological Advancement: Did the process aim to generate new scientific or technological knowledge advancing underlying capability (noting that failed experiments advancing technical knowledge qualify, whereas commercial novelty built with standard techniques does not)?
Contemporaneous Documentation: Were records of the hypotheses tested, experimental iterations, and analytical conclusions generated contemporaneously as the work progressed?

body.text: Audit Defence, Administrative Escalation, and Gross Negligence Penalties

Although well-substantiated claims experience strong acceptance (with industry reporting noting a 91% acceptance rate as filed or with minor adjustments in 2023–2024), claimants must maintain dated contemporaneous artefacts—source-code commits, pull requests, engineering tickets, experimental test logs, lab notebooks, employee time records, contractor agreements, and post-December 15, 2024 equipment operating-time logs proving ≥90% ASA or >50% SUE/lease utilization. Disputed CRA review proposals may be escalated administratively under the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns, challenged via a formal Notice of Objection, and appealed to the Tax Court of Canada, while overstated or fabricated claims face severe statutory penalties under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025).
